title: No way(mo) out
text: Last week, the UK Government opened applications for companies to begin operating autonomous taxi, bus, and ride-hailing services, with a view that customers will be able to begin using the services by the end of this year. Waymo’s distinctive white vehicles have already been prowling the streets of London for several months as they map its streets, recently even without their human safety drivers, as they map the streets. While there’s a lot of understandable hype building around these futuristic cars, I don’t think they’re the transportation panacea people might be expecting.

title: No way(mo) out
text:
Road safety
Road safety is one of the most prominently cited benefits of autonomous vehicles (AVs). According to the Department for Transport, 88% of all collisions are caused by human error, including “drink driving, speeding, tiredness and inattention”. It stands to reason that we could therefore eliminate the vast majority of road collisions by using AVs. Moreover, Waymo’s own safety research, based on trials in the USA, show that using their AVs leads to a 92% decrease in collisions and a 82% decrease in serious injury caused by collisions.
These statistics are fantastic, and it cannot be denied that reducing road collisions is objectively a good thing. However, AVs are not the only way to achieve this. It has been shown that reducing speed limits to 20mph significantly reduces rates of collisions and serious injury from collisions with studies reporting up to 20-60% reductions in injuries and fatalities across the UK. Moreover, reducing the bonnet height of cars is essential for reducing fatal collisions: one study found that a 10cm increase in bonnet height increases the risk of death to pedestrians and cyclists by 27%. With a car population that has grown in height by over 16cm since 2010, such that children as old as 9 are invisible from the driver’s seat, we should be urgently passing regulations to limit vehicle bonnet height.
Ignoring these easy wins while embracing the hype of novelty robotaxis seems short sighted and symptomatic of deep-set car-brain. Reducing speeds and reducing bonnet heights are fast, simple, and sure-fire ways to reduce road collisions, and reducing the number of cars on the roads would go a step further again. After all, 100% of car collisions involve cars.

title: No way(mo) out
text:
Sustainability
Waymo’s website also discusses the green credentials of electric AVs. Many argue that, since these electric vehicles are a shared fleet, they will be able to replace private car journeys and take other cars off the roads. This echoes remarkably well what was said about Uber coming to our streets several years ago. Yet, it has been shown that Uber has had no such effect, and has in fact increased vehicle miles travelled and even contributed greater emissions per trip overall as drivers circle cities waiting for their next fare. While Waymo have addressed this specifically, stating that they “limit empty miles” by ensuring unused vehicles will be directed to park or return to the distribution depot, there’s no convincing evidence that these measures will be effective (and where is there to park in central London!?). Though these new AVs are electric - thus definitively “sustainable” according to Waymo - these additional miles are hardly eco-friendly; all vehicles generate pollution from tires and brake pads, and heavier EVs are in fact the worst offenders.
Moreover, the introduction of AVs may deter cyclists from using our streets. Cyclists are already vulnerable road users, with nearly half of cyclists feeling unsafe on the roads of London today, and concerns are being raised that they may be at greater risk with AVs on the roads. In particular, there have been reports of Waymo vehicles stopping and picking up passengers in bike lanes (as well as flagrantly breaking road rules). In 2026, Waymo allegedly announced that expecting their cars to respect cycle lanes was “too high a bar”.
Surely, then, a better transport solution would reduce mileage, encourage cycling, and reduce pollution. In practice, this looks like fewer cars and a system oriented towards active travel and (electric) public transport instead; more cars cannot be the answer.

title: No way(mo) out
text:
Traffic efficiency
Similarly, we are promised that autonomous fleets will improve traffic efficiency by reducing unnecessary congestion. This will be achieved in several ways, such as by reducing phantom traffic caused by human error or through connected vehicles communicating with each other in real-time to optimise traffic flow.
These positive effects on congestion of (connected) AVs have been studied widely and are well-documented (see here and here for examples). But, aside from the afore-mentioned empty miles issue, there is potential for (short-term) congestion increase due to induced demand (similar to what is a well-observed phenomenon with road widening). While some argue this temporary congestion increase will eventually subside as we magically overcome our love of private vehicles and shift to an entirely shared fleet of cars, I think we’re again fundamentally looking to solve the wrong problem. Instead of asking how we can reduce congestion given the transport system stays the same, we should be asking how can we reduce congestion altogether. At the end of the day, congestion consists of vehicles (you’re not IN traffic, you ARE traffic). Putting more cars on the road cannot remove congestion. Only reducing the number cars on the roads can do this.

title: No way(mo) out
text:
Accessibility
Finally, AVs are praised for their accessibility credentials, and understandably so. AVs open up car use for those who are unable to drive, for example due to disability or age. These vehicles facilitate independent travel, where previously people have had to rely heavily on insufficient public transport, asking favours from friends and family, or simply missing out.
However, as it stands, AV offerings are not designed to help the most vulnerable. A Waymo spokesperson described fares as “competitive” but “premium”, indicating that trips in these vehicles will not be affordable for general everyday use. In the UK, the poverty rate for disabled people is consistently higher than non-disabled people and employment rates are significantly lower for disabled people (52.8% compared with 82.5% for non-disabled people). With current ride-hailing app users found to be predominantly young, employed people, and with middle-income young people the most likely to adopt shared AV use, we cannot assume that using robotaxis will be of great immediate benefit to the most vulnerable. Moreover, in 2024, only 11% of private hire vehicles in England were wheelchair accessible.
In fact, the introduction and popularisation of AVs may exclude these most vulnerable members of society even more. As Giulio Mattioli describes: “the self-reinforcing cycle of car dependence results in an increasing intensity of car deprivation for a decreasing proportion of the population”. Those who do not drive and cannot afford a AV will be at even greater disadvantage as the ratchet of social car dependence tightens.
Waymo claiming to be a positive step for increasing transport accessibility is therefore, at best a premature and overly-optimistic assessment and at worst a co-opting of accessibility language to gain social credit. Means-tested pricing or subsidies for the most vulnerable may help to truly improve accessibility. But in general, more cars on the roads only deepens the core of the problem.

title: No way(mo) out
text:
Final thoughts
Yes, AVs are amazing technology and objectively cool. But we know better than to equate “cool” with “good”. To quote Paris Marx in his fantastic book “Road to Nowhere”: “addressing the inequities and harms of our world does not require the invention of new technologies; it requires a new politics that recognises economic growth and technological innovation do not guarantee social progress”.
In summary, I think we’ve lost sight of what the true goal is. We should not be asking if AVs on the roads will improve certain elements of driving. We should be asking how to meaningfully improve people’s lives through fairer, more accessible, and more equitable transport. Improving the way we use cars is a small change of the existing system. We need a big change in the system itself.

title: About
text:
Hi, I’m Maria and I’m a PhD student at CASA UCL in the City Modelling Lab.
I’m studying the social and spatial inequalities in transport, especially in the context of the UK’s EV transition through the twin climate and inequality crises. I have a particular focus on car dependence and transport flexibility. I have a particularly strong (negative) feeling towards SUVs in cities. In former lives I played classical flute, studied physics and worked as an energy consultant in a Big Company. In current life I’m a (very) amateur forager, nature enthusiast, climate activist, cryptic crossworder and vegan baked goods enjoyer.

title: Freedom on the roads: a short story
text:
I climb into my car in the enormous grey office car park as the clock hits 7.51pm. God, I hate it in there – being in my little cubicle all day, confined in a box, surrounded by paperwork and sexist managers. It’s just senseless pen-pushing and box-ticking bureaucracy, but somehow administered in such a strict hierarchy of control and painstaking scrutiny. It’s suffocating.
I’m so relieved to be out of there and in my car, my own little pocket of freedom and lawlessness. I like to imagine I’m cruising through the countryside, like in those old movies, with none of this day-to-day bullshit to deal with. Just me and the road and all of the world at my fingertips. I’m free, I’m alone, and I answer to nobody.
THUNK.
That goddamn pothole on Clementine Avenue. How have they not fixed that yet? It’s been weeks, I swear. Someone should sort that out before there’s an accident. I worry the jolt from the pothole encounter must have shaken something loose, as a tinny rattling starts emerging from the front of the car. Then I remember I left some coins in the passenger seat door pocket and they must be rattling around in there. Thank god – I have no idea how cars really work I hate having to deal with Andrea at the shop. She’s always taking the piss that I’m not self-sufficient and can’t even change a tyre and that’s not very feminist of me or whatever. I got better things to do than figure out how all those pipes and engines work. That’s Andrea’s job, and I pay her to do it.
Anyways – tonight is the night! Daphne has organized for all of us to go dancing at the new venue on the outskirts of town for her 30th. I’m really excited. It’s been ages since I went dancing and I’ve heard some good things about this venue. They apparently serve every cocktail under the sun, but with a silly animal-themed name like Meowtini or something. Daphne loves that novelty stuff. I’m heading there straight from work so I try to get into the party spirit by cranking up the radio and reach over to get my rave shades out of the glovebox. My MOT reminder letter falls out of the compartment where I stashed it the other day. Shit. Looks like I’m going to have to deal with Andrea next week anyways. To be honest, I can’t believe my ancient janky car hasn’t failed on the environmental side of things given the smoky fumes that come out the back sometimes. Maybe this is the year I’ll have to upgrade. I sigh, wishing that life didn’t have to be so full of endless admin.
I hit the accelerator and open the window a crack to feel the wind in my hair and relax into the drive as I cruise on the dual carriageway. There’s a flash as I pass the speed camera. I look down at my speedometer and it says 75mph. GODDAMIT. Those bright yellow boxy bastards. Ughh, ANPR can eat my shorts. I hate this surveillance nonsense, like, just chill already. It’s not like an extra 5mph is hurting anyone. I reluctantly bring my speed down to just under 70mph, feeling like I have had my wings clipped or a tight leash clamped around my neck.
Still, it’s better than taking the bus. At least I’m not waiting at that stop for 20 minutes, not knowing if or when that hulking green rectangle will pull up. I know that I’ll be at the venue in exactly – I check GoogleMaps for the ETA – 57 minutes. Wait, what?? I swear it said less than 30 minutes last time I looked. I noticed that the route marker on the map had turned red for the next mile or so and as I reached the top of the shallow hill in the road I’d been climbing, an ocean of static car backsides emerged, each jeering at me with their red twinkling eyes through the dusk. I was already running late but this extra delay meant Daphne would be mad.
“Hey, Siri. Text Daphne saying”Hey Daphne so sorry I’m gonna be about half an hour late cos of mega traffic. I’ll buy you a drink to make up for it! Hyped to boogie with you soon babe”“.
Just over half an hour later, I emerge out of the congestion and the road speed picks up again. I see on the hard shoulder the wreckage of two cars – their collision must have caused the traffic. Their drivers were long gone, but the physical damage was clear. I hope they’re all okay. People should be more careful, really. I finally make it to the venue and start looking for somewhere to park. There’s no designated car park, so I stalk the side roads for about 15 minutes until I find a space between two driveways. It’s a narrow street so I squeeze partly onto the pavement, hoping that the traffic wardens won’t be coming round here on a Friday night. I pay at the machine – they’ve not upgraded to the app system here it seems – and it comes to nearly a tenner. Absolute rip-off for a dark street with a dusting of what looks like the glass of car windows all across the pavement. I double check that I locked the car and power walk in to the venue.
“Hey girl!! Omg happy birthday!!! Sorry I’m so late, traffic and all, you know how it is. Lemme get you a drink – what you having?” I greet Daphne. She squeezes me and, after pretending to scold me for my lateness, places her order. I leave her to the dancefloor and head over to the bar.
“Hey man, I’ll have one um… Kitty Colada and one diet coke please.”
“ID?” The bartender asked. I’m always flattered to be ID-ed in my late twenties.
“Yeah, course. Here you go.” I hand over my driving license. The bartender examines it for longer than he should. I notice his name is Josh on his nametag.
“It’s a bad picture haha, the lighting is terrible,” I joke self-consciously.
“No no, it’s not that! I think you live on the same street as my Nan is all! And your birthday is like 2 days off from mine! Small world hey!” Josh smiles disarmingly but I’m annoyed.
I can’t tell if this is an extremely poor attempt at flirting with me but regardless, it was creepy. We all know the unspoken agreement that you just check I’m over 18 and ignore all the actual personal information on there. Just because the DVLA needs all my details, it doesn’t mean you should know it Josh. I snatched my ID back and shut him down as quickly as I could. “Hah, yeah, small world. Bye.”
I skip back to Daphne and the gang. “What, you just got a diet coke? C’mon the cocktails are so good here, and we’re celebrating” Daphne whines jokingly. “Yeah, but I’m driving remember? Can’t drink and drive you all home can I!” “Hey don’t blame me!” Chimes in one of Daphne’s work friends. “I’m catching the bus home!” Daphne and I meet eyes and laugh as if to say “This guy”. He’s the worst. We dance to the cheesy pop hits until the early hours when Daphne decides she’s finally ready for some chips and bed. I drive her and a couple others to their doors and make sure they get home okay. Annoying that I’m the designated driver, but it’s only fair that it’s my turn.
I finally return home. I’m absolutely exhausted yet totally wired. That was a lot of time behind the wheel; I always find driving at night stressful, especially with 3 drunk friends and 3 ketchup-laden boxes of chips whirling around. It’s been a long day. I enter my front door, I notice a pile of post on the floor. It’s mostly junk but amongst the takeout menus and local political canvassing, I spot a letter from my car insurance company. I wince, remembering the yellow camera’s flash and the inevitable increase of my premium.
Screw it, I’m not dealing with that tonight. I’m going to go for a walk to clear my head and decompress before bed.
I turn 180 degrees back into the cool night air. As I walk along my street, I notice that each house has at least one metal cubicle parked up outside. Looks like everyone here has their own pocket of freedom to go where they want, when they want. If they can afford it. If they follow the rules correctly, if the lights and signs and roads are maintained properly, if they have somewhere to park at the other end.
I pick my way between the cars parked on the pavement, barely able to navigate through them, wondering how Mrs Halliday at 42 gets through here with her Zimmer frame. I can hear the revving of a sports car racing down the main road the next street over, and after a couple of seconds the smell of toxic exhaust fumes fills my nostrils. They’re definitely not passing their next MOT I chuckle to myself.
I cross the road to where the footpath towards the common begins.
I emerge from the blue-white LED-lit path into the common as the sun’s warm glow begins to fill the sky and walk meanderingly through the trees, across the grassy lawns. The birds are beginning their morning song, and the planted flowerbeds sparkle pink-red in the dew. I take a deep breath. I am not registered, taxed, insured, or restricted to a painted lane.
For the first time in a long time I finally feel free.
